title: Lidar: seeing with light
about: How a spinning laser maps a room, like a robot vacuum or a self-driving car.

html: Lidar works like ultrasonic, but it uses a laser instead of sound.
LIDAR stands for LIght Detection And Ranging. Most lidars fire a tiny flash of invisible laser light and time how long the reflection takes to come back.
Light is about 870,000 times faster than sound. It travels about 30 cm in one nanosecond (ns), a billionth of a second. So lidar needs a super fast timer.
A laser beam is thin, so it measures one exact spot. To see the whole room, many lidars spin and measure thousands of spots every second.
Each measurement is one dot. Put the dots together and you get a map called a point cloud.
• Robot vacuums: on many of them, the round bump on top is a spinning lidar that maps your house.
• Self-driving cars: many use lidar to spot cars, bikes, and people all around them.
• Some phones have a tiny lidar that measures rooms and helps the camera focus in the dark.
• Behind things. The laser stops at the first thing it hits. That's why you had to drive around the mystery shape.
• Clear glass. The laser goes right through, so a glass door can look like an open doorway.
• Mirrors bounce the laser away, and fog or heavy rain scatters it.

steps.q: Light travels about 30 cm every nanosecond. A laser flash comes back after 20 nanoseconds. How far away is the object?
steps.explain: In 20 ns light goes 20 × 0.3 m = 6 m. That's there and back, so the object is 3 m away.

steps.q: Why does a robot vacuum's lidar spin?
options: To measure in every direction and build a map
steps.explain: One laser beam measures one spot. Spinning sweeps it all the way around, thousands of times, to map the room.

steps.q: In the mystery room, why did you have to drive around the shape?
options: Lidar only sees the sides its laser can reach
steps.explain: The laser can't go through things, so the back of the shape stays hidden until you look from another side.
